weeks.title: Thousands, hundreds, tens and ones

spell.rule: Prefixes in- and im- mean 'not'; im- goes before words starting with m or p (incorrect, invisible, impossible, impatient, immature)

weeks.read: Borrow a collection of myths and legends from the library to dip into this half term; read one myth aloud together each evening.

days.ma: Draw a place value chart with columns Th, H, T and O. Use buttons or paper scraps as counters (a counter in the Th column is worth 1000). Build 3452, 2076 and 4500 and say what each digit is worth – in 2076 the 0 means there are no hundreds.
days.en: Start the year with myths. Read a Greek or Norse myth aloud together, then list what makes it a myth: gods or magical beings, a hero, a quest, a monster, or an explanation of something in nature.

days.ma: Partition 4637 in the usual way (4000 + 600 + 30 + 7) and then two other ways, such as 3000 + 1600 + 30 + 7 or 4000 + 500 + 137. Prove each one on the counter chart, then try 5208.
days.en: Handwriting warm-up: write the joins 'ight', 'ough' and 'ss' five times each, then copy 'I believe the hero will win.' twice, keeping ascenders and descenders well clear of the lines above and below.

days.ma: Show 2745 four ways on one sheet: in words, on the chart, as a partitioned sum, and as a rough mark on a 0 to 10 000 line drawn along the top of the page. Which way makes the number easiest to picture?
days.en: Spelling: add in- or im- to correct, visible, possible, patient, mature and perfect. Spot the pattern (im- before m and p), say what each new word means and write two of them in sentences.

days.ma: Mystery number: give clues such as 'I have 6 thousands and no hundreds; my ones digit is 4 and my tens digit is double that.' Your child writes 6084, then makes up clues for a number for you to find.
days.en: Grammar words: copy out one paragraph of the myth. Underline nouns in one colour, verbs in another and adjectives in a third, and circle any adverbs or conjunctions. Use the proper names when talking about your choices.

days.ma: Friday check: What is the 7 worth in 7215? Partition 3906 two ways. Write four thousand and sixty in numerals. Which digit is in the hundreds place in 5482? Mark together and redo any slips.
days.en: Dictation: read aloud 'I am certain the monster is invisible.' and 'Do you believe it is impossible?' Your child writes them from memory, then checks capitals, punctuation and the spellings of certain and believe.

weeks.title: Roman numerals, counting in 1000s and 1000 more or less

spell.rule: Prefixes il- (before l) and ir- (before r) also mean 'not' (illegal, illegible, illogical, irregular, irresponsible, irrelevant)

weeks.read: Carry on with the myths collection, choosing one with a monster or a quest to read independently.

days.ma: Roman numerals: write I, V, X, L and C with their values (1, 5, 10, 50, 100). Build 3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 19 and 40 together, noticing that a smaller numeral before a larger one means subtract (IV = 4, XL = 40).
days.en: Read a myth chapter. Stop at an exciting moment and ask: 'How is the hero feeling? Which words tell you?' Then predict what will happen next and give a reason from the text.

days.ma: Roman numeral hunt: look for numerals on clock faces, old buildings in photos, book chapter headings or film credits. Read 6 found or invented numerals (e.g. XXVII, LXIV, XCIX) and write each in our digits. Talk about how the Romans had no symbol for zero, which is why our place value system is easier.
days.en: Fronted adverbials: a fronted adverbial is a phrase at the start of a sentence telling when, where or how. Write three: 'Before dawn, the hero set off.' 'Deep in the cave, …' 'Without a sound, …' and finish them, remembering the comma.

days.ma: Count in 1000s from 0 to 10 000 and back, then from 3250 to 9250. Next play '1000 more, 1000 less': you say 4718, your child says 5718 and 3718. Include tricky ones like 9056 (1000 more is 10 056).
days.en: Spelling: add il- or ir- to legal, legible, logical, regular, responsible and relevant. Sort them into il- and ir- words and write 'It is illegal to build there.'

days.ma: Counting in 25s: count from 0 to 300 in 25s, clapping on each hundred. Link to money: 4 quarters of £1 is 100p, so 25, 50, 75, 100. Then count back from 500 in 25s.
days.en: Word roots: take the root word 'build' and make builder, building, rebuild and built. Do the same for 'legal' (illegal, legally). Use a dictionary to check any you are unsure of.

days.ma: Friday check: Write 9, 14, 40 and 76 in Roman numerals; read XXXIX and LXXXV. What is 1000 more than 6450? 1000 less than 2009? Count on four 25s from 175. Mark and correct together.
days.en: Dictation: 'Before sunset, the giants began to build a wall.' and 'Is the writing illegible?' Check the comma after the fronted adverbial, the question mark and the spelling of build.

weeks.title: Comparing and ordering numbers to 10 000

spell.rule: The s sound spelt sc, a pattern from Latin (science, scene, discipline, fascinate, crescent, scissors)

weeks.read: A myth or legend retold as a picture book or comic strip, to compare with the longer versions.

days.ma: Write 4589, 4859, 4598, 5489 and 4958 on scraps. Order them smallest to largest by comparing thousands first, then hundreds, then tens. Then use < and > to compare pairs.
days.en: Dictionary race: give your child five words from the myth (scene, fascinate, creature, quest, temple). Using the first two or three letters, they find each one and read out its meaning. Time each search and try to beat it.

days.ma: Number line estimating: draw a 0 to 10 000 line and mark 5000 in the middle. Your child marks where 2500, 7200, 9900 and 450 roughly go, then explains how they decided.
days.en: Spelling: read and sort science, scene, discipline, fascinate, crescent and scissors. Say each aloud and note the silent c after s. Learn century and centre with look–say–cover–write–check, and spot the soft c in both.

days.ma: Practical problem: find four 4-digit numbers around the home (a car mileage, a year on a coin, a page count, a price in pence). Order them, then round each to the nearest thousand to see which are close together.
days.en: Read a myth chapter. Find two places where a character's actions show a feeling without the word for the feeling being used. Explain the inference: 'She clenched her fists, so I think she was angry.'

days.ma: Tables warm-up: 2 minutes of mixed 3, 4 and 8 times table questions, said aloud. Then use digit cards 2, 0, 7 and 5 to make the largest and smallest 4-digit numbers and all those between 5000 and 6000.
days.en: Conjunctions: write three sentences about the myth using although, because and when, e.g. 'Although the hero was tired, she kept climbing.' Talk about whether the conjunction starts the sentence or joins the middle.

days.ma: Friday check: Order 3071, 3701, 3017, 3170. Which is greater, 6099 or 6909? Mark 7500 on a 0 to 10 000 line. Make the smallest number from 8, 1, 4 and 0 that does not start with 0. Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'In the centre of the scene stood a fascinating temple.' and 'It had been there for a century.' Your child writes, then checks the comma, the sc words and the spellings of centre and century.

weeks.title: Rounding to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000

spell.rule: Homophones: accept/except, affect/effect, ball/bawl, berry/bury

weeks.read: Read a second myth from a different culture (for example Egyptian or Norse) and compare the heroes.

days.ma: Rounding on a number line: draw a line from 3700 to 3800. Mark 3742 and decide whether it is nearer 3700 or 3800. Do the same for 3750 (agree the rule: halfway rounds up) and 3768.
days.en: Plan a myth: talk about how myths are built (opening, a problem, a quest, a battle or test, an ending that explains something). Draw a five-box story map for a new myth explaining why the moon changes shape.

days.ma: Round 6385 to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000 (6390, 6400, 6000). Repeat with 2950 and 8049. Talk about why 2950 rounds to 3000 to the nearest hundred.
days.en: Homophones: write accept/except, affect/effect, ball/bawl and berry/bury on cards. Read sentences aloud ('Everyone came ___ the cat.') and your child holds up the right spelling, then writes two sentences of their own.

days.ma: Estimate first: 'About how many steps from the front door to the end of the road?' Count or measure, then round the answer to the nearest 10 and 100. Then round some prices in pence from a receipt to the nearest 10p and nearest pound.
days.en: Read on in the myth. Ask your child to summarise the last two paragraphs in one sentence each, then explain why they think the writer split the text there.

days.ma: Rounding game: roll two dice or use digit cards to make a 4-digit number; each player rounds to the nearest 1000, 100 and 10. A point for each correct answer. Finish with 2 minutes of 6 times table, building from facts already known (6 × 4 is double 3 × 4).
days.en: Handwriting: copy the opening line of your myth plan in best joined writing, checking that downstrokes are parallel and letters are evenly spaced. Then copy it again and compare.

days.ma: Friday check: Round 4527 to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000. Which numbers round to 3000 to the nearest 1000: 2499, 2500, 3499, 3500? Round £4.67 to the nearest pound. Mark and correct together.
days.en: Dictation: 'I thought the hero caught the ball.' and 'Did the storm affect everyone except the king?' Check homophones, the question mark and the spellings of caught and thought.

weeks.title: Negative numbers and counting in 6s, 7s, 9s and 25s

spell.rule: The suffix -ous (poisonous, dangerous, mountainous, famous, nervous); keep the root word where you can

weeks.read: A myth read aloud by an adult in the evenings, with your child reading the dialogue parts.

days.ma: Draw a vertical number line from -10 to 10 like a thermometer. Count back from 6 to -6, then forward from -8 to 3. Talk about temperatures below zero: 'It is 2 °C and it falls 5 degrees. What is it now?'
days.en: Draft the opening of your myth (one paragraph): introduce the setting and hero. Use a fronted adverbial such as 'Long ago, …' or 'High in the mountains, …' and an expanded noun phrase such as 'a nervous young shepherd with a wooden flute'.

days.ma: Negative number problems: the freezer is -18 °C and the fridge is 4 °C – how much warmer is the fridge? Make up two more using the vertical line. Then count back in 25s from 100 to -100.
days.en: Paragraphs: write the next paragraph of the myth, where the problem begins. Talk first about why we start a new paragraph (new time, new place, new event or a new person speaking).

days.ma: Count in 6s, 7s and 9s to 60, 70 and 90 using fingers. Spot the 9s pattern: tens go up by 1 and ones go down by 1. Write the 9s with the tens digits 0–8 in one column and the ones 9–1 in the next.
days.en: Spelling: add -ous to danger, poison, mountain and fame (fame drops the e). Talk about which roots change. Then learn various and ordinary, noticing the -ous in various.

days.ma: Counting stick game: draw a line marked with 11 notches. Point to notches at random while your child says the multiple of 7 (0, 7, 14 …). Then do the same for 6s and 25s.
days.en: Draft the third paragraph, where the hero faces the test. Use various ways to start sentences: a fronted adverbial, a conjunction such as 'When …', and a pronoun instead of repeating the hero's name.

days.ma: Friday check: Count back from 3 in 2s to -7. What is 4 less than -1? Fill the gaps: 18, 24, __, 36; 63, 54, __, 36; 150, 175, __, 225. The temperature rises from -3 °C to 5 °C – by how much? Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'Various dangerous creatures lived in the mountains.' and 'The ordinary boy was nervous.' Check full stops, capitals and the spellings of various and ordinary.

weeks.title: Adding 4-digit numbers in columns

spell.rule: More -ous: words ending -our change to -or before -ous (humour → humorous, glamour → glamorous, vigour → vigorous), and -eous/-ious (courageous, outrageous, serious, obvious, curious)

weeks.read: Your child chooses a fiction book from the library for the rest of the half term – the first pick of the year.

days.ma: Column addition with no exchanges: 3421 + 2354. Line up thousands, hundreds, tens and ones and add from the ones. Use counters on the chart for the first one, then try 4132 + 5617 on paper.
days.en: Finish the myth with an ending paragraph that explains something in nature (why the moon changes shape). Read the whole draft aloud to check it makes sense.

days.ma: Column addition with exchanges: 2768 + 1457. When a column makes ten or more, exchange ten ones for one ten (and so on), writing the small 1 under the next column. Estimate first: 2800 + 1500 = 4300.
days.en: Evaluate: re-read the myth together. Find one sentence to make more exciting by changing a verb or adding an adverbial, and one place where 'he' or 'she' is unclear and the noun should be used.

days.ma: Inverse check: after 3586 + 2747 = 6333, subtract 2747 from 6333 to see you get back to 3586. Talk about how an estimate (3600 + 2700) also shows whether the answer is sensible.
days.en: Spelling: add -ous to humour, glamour, courage, outrage and vary; sort into 'drop u' and 'keep e' words. Then learn peculiar using look–say–cover–write–check.

days.ma: Real-life adding: find two 3- or 4-digit numbers at home, such as the pages in two books or the calories on two food packets, and add them in columns. Then a 2-minute mixed tables warm-up on 3s, 4s and 6s.
days.en: Proof-read the myth for spelling and punctuation. Use a dictionary for at least two words. Then copy the best paragraph in neat joined handwriting.

days.ma: Friday check: 4526 + 3271; 3678 + 2545; estimate then check 1999 + 2864. Is 5428 + 3916 more or less than 9000? Mark together and use the inverse to check one answer.
days.en: Read the myth aloud to the family, changing your voice for the monster and slowing down at the tense moment. Then dictation: 'The curious monster had a peculiar, humorous laugh.'

weeks.title: Consolidation: place value, rounding and addition

spell.rule: Revise this half term: in-/im-, il-/ir-, sc for s, homophones, -ous endings

weeks.read: Re-read a favourite myth from this half term and prepare a passage to read aloud with expression.

days.ma: Place value relay: say 'five thousand and forty-six'. Your child writes it, partitions it, writes it 1000 more and 1000 less and rounds it to the nearest 100. Repeat with 7809 and 2950.
days.en: Spelling round-up: read 10 words from this half term (impossible, illegal, science, various, believe, centre, thought, peculiar, famous, irregular). Your child writes them; tick and practise any slips.

days.ma: Ordering and negatives: order 6052, 6520, 6205, 6250 and place them on a 6000–7000 line. Then count back in 3s from 10 to -11.
days.en: Grammar recap: write a sentence with a fronted adverbial and comma, a sentence with 'although', and one with an expanded noun phrase. Name each feature as you share them.

days.ma: Mental and written mix: 4762 + 1000, 6305 – 1000, 3999 + 1, then a column sum with two exchanges, 3687 + 4545, with an estimate and inverse check.
days.en: Homophone challenge: use accept, except, affect, effect, bury and berry in a silly short story of four sentences. Proof-read it together.

days.ma: Roman numeral and rounding quiz: write XLVIII, LXXIV and XCIX in digits; write 33 and 59 in Roman numerals; round 8451 to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000.
days.en: Book chat: each person names the best myth from this half term and gives two reasons. Listen without interrupting, then ask the other person one question about their choice.

days.ma: Half-term check: 10 mixed questions you write, e.g. the value of 4 in 4310; 1000 less than 3025; round 5649 to the nearest 100; -2 + 5; 2878 + 3456; XC in digits. Celebrate what is secure and note anything to revisit.
days.en: Dictation: 'Before dawn, the hero had to decide.' and 'It was impossible to believe the peculiar scene.' Then a neat copy in best joined handwriting.

weeks.title: Subtracting 4-digit numbers in columns

spell.rule: The suffix -tion: when the root word ends in t or te, add -ion (invent → invention, act → action, complete → completion, hesitate → hesitation)

weeks.read: A non-fiction book about how something works (the human body, volcanoes, the water cycle) from the library or home shelf.

days.ma: Column subtraction with no exchanges: 5876 – 2453. Then with one exchange: 4352 – 1728, exchanging a ten for ten ones. Model the first on the place value chart with counters.
days.en: Start a non-fiction unit. Look at a fact book together: find the contents page, index, headings, sub-headings, diagrams and glossary. Talk about why each feature is there.

days.ma: Exchanging across a zero: 6005 – 2378 is the trickiest kind. Work through it slowly on the chart (exchange a thousand for ten hundreds, a hundred for ten tens, a ten for ten ones), then try 4030 – 1564.
days.en: Retrieval: choose one page of the fact book. Write five questions whose answers are on the page (who, what, where, when, how). Swap and answer each other's, writing the answers in full sentences.

days.ma: Check by adding: after 7214 – 3586 = 3628, add 3628 + 3586 to get back to 7214. Then estimate 7214 – 3586 as 7200 – 3600 to see the answer is about 3600.
days.en: Spelling: add -tion to invent, act, complete, hesitate, inject and educate (dropping the final e). Learn mention and complete with look–say–cover–write–check.

days.ma: Subtraction at home: find the year on a coin or packet, then work out how many years ago that was in columns. Then find the difference between two 4-digit numbers on food packets or a receipt total in pence.
days.en: Standard English: talk about 'we was' versus 'we were' and 'I done it' versus 'I did it'. Correct five sentences you write with mistakes, e.g. 'They was going home.', 'She done her homework.'

days.ma: Friday check: 6875 – 3542; 5213 – 2786; 7000 – 3456. Use addition to check one of them. Estimate 8015 – 2987. Mark together and redo any slips.
days.en: Dictation: 'We were asked to mention the invention.' and 'Did you complete the action?' Check standard English, the -tion words and the spellings of mention and complete.

weeks.title: Two-step addition and subtraction problems

spell.rule: The suffix -sion: when the root word ends in d, de or se, use -sion (expand → expansion, extend → extension, comprehend → comprehension, tense → tension, divide → division, decide → decision)

weeks.read: Carry on with the non-fiction book, choosing a second one on the same topic to compare facts.

days.ma: Two-step problem: 'A school has 2450 pencils. It buys 1375 more, then gives 1600 to another school. How many now?' Draw a bar model, decide the operations, estimate, then calculate.
days.en: Plan an explanation text, such as 'How water gets from the sky to the tap'. Look at a fact book page to see how it is organised, then plan headings and the order of the steps in a flow chart.

days.ma: Choose the method: for each question decide 'mental or columns?' and say why – 3000 – 1, 4562 + 2999, 5728 – 3496, 1250 + 1250. Then do them.
days.en: Spelling: change extend, expand, comprehend, tense, divide and decide into -sion words. Sort by sound (sh or zh). Learn occasion(ally) and use occasionally in a sentence.

days.ma: Real-life problem: 'A family drives 1245 miles on holiday one year and 368 fewer miles the next. How many miles in the two years altogether?' Estimate first, solve, then check with the inverse.
days.en: Retrieval: from the second fact book, find three facts that are the same as in the first book and one that is different. Record them in a two-column table.

days.ma: Make your own two-step problem using numbers from the home (pages in books, steps walked, prices in pence). Swap with a grown-up and solve each other's, explaining which operations you chose and why.
days.en: Grammar words: in a fact book paragraph, find a determiner (the, a, some, every), a pronoun, a preposition and an adverbial. Label them, then find a sentence with two clauses and name the conjunction.

days.ma: Friday check: 'A shop had 3500 cards, sold 1278 and then received 900 more. How many now?' Plus 4725 + 2386 and 6003 – 2475 with estimates. Mark together and check one answer with the inverse.
days.en: Dictation: 'Occasionally, the river makes a huge expansion across the valley.' and 'What was your decision?' Check the fronted adverbial comma and the -sion spellings.

weeks.title: Area: counting squares

spell.rule: The suffix -ssion: when the root word ends in ss or mit, use -ssion (express → expression, discuss → discussion, permit → permission, admit → admission)

weeks.read: A fact book with diagrams and labels, to borrow ideas for presenting your explanation text.

days.ma: Area is the space a flat shape covers. Draw shapes on squared paper (or draw a 1 cm grid with a ruler) and find their areas by counting squares, including an L-shape. Write answers as 'squares' or 'cm²'.
days.en: Draft the explanation text from last week: write a title, an introduction saying what you will explain, and the first step under a sub-heading. Use time adverbials such as 'First,', 'After that,'.

days.ma: Make shapes with an area of 12 squares: how many different rectangles and other rectilinear shapes can you draw? Do they all look the same size? Talk about how same area does not mean same shape.
days.en: Draft the next two steps under sub-headings. Add a labelled diagram. Check you are using standard English, e.g. 'The clouds were heavy', not 'The clouds was heavy'.

days.ma: Area of real things: use sticky notes, playing cards or coasters of the same size to cover a book, a placemat and a tray. Count how many each takes and compare. Which has the greatest area?
days.en: Spelling: change express, discuss, permit, admit, possess and impress into -ssion words. Write 'Do you have permission to touch my possession?'

days.ma: Compare areas: draw two shapes on squared paper with areas of 15 and 18 squares. Which is bigger and by how much? Then 2 minutes of 6 times table and 3 minutes of 9 times table questions.
days.en: Evaluate and edit: read the explanation aloud. Is each step clear? Add a 'Did you know?' fact box and change any unclear pronouns to nouns.

days.ma: Friday check: find the area of three shapes you draw on squared paper (one rectangle, one L-shape, one with a hole). Draw a shape with an area of 10 squares. Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'After the discussion, we were given permission.' and 'The diagram showed the clouds.' Then copy the title and introduction of the explanation in neat joined handwriting.

weeks.title: The 6, 9 and 3 times tables

spell.rule: The suffix -cian is used for jobs and people, often from root words ending in c or cs (music → musician, magic → magician, electric → electrician, politics → politician)

weeks.read: A story with lots of dialogue between characters, read aloud together with different voices.

days.ma: 6 times table: write the 3s, then double each answer to get the 6s. Chant the 6s forwards and backwards, then answer 10 mixed 6s questions (7 × 6, 6 × 9, 42 ÷ 6 …) using fingers to track.
days.en: Read a chapter of a story with dialogue. Find the speech marks (inverted commas) and talk about where the words actually spoken begin and end, and where the comma or question mark goes.

days.ma: 9 times table: use the finger trick (hold up 10 fingers, fold down the third for 3 × 9, leaving 2 tens and 7 ones = 27). Then work out 9 × n as 10 × n – n (9 × 8 = 80 – 8).
days.en: Direct speech rules: copy 'Hurry up,' said Mum. and 'Where are we going?' asked the boy. Point out the comma or question mark inside the closing inverted commas. Write three of your own.

days.ma: Facts and their families: from 6 × 7 = 42, write 7 × 6 = 42, 42 ÷ 6 = 7 and 42 ÷ 7 = 6. Do the same for 9 × 8 and 6 × 12. Talk about how the order of multiplying doesn't matter.
days.en: Spelling: add -cian to music, magic, electric, politics and mathematics. What do the words have in common? Learn medicine and particular with look–say–cover–write–check.

days.ma: Kitchen game: deal cards from a pack (picture cards removed, ace = 1). Multiply each by 6 or 9 as fast as you can, keeping score. Then count in 6s and 9s to 108 while bouncing a ball.
days.en: Reporting clause first: write 'The magician said, "Watch closely."' Notice the comma before the inverted commas. Then write a short conversation between a musician and a magician using both styles.

days.ma: Friday check: 15 mixed 3, 6 and 9 times tables and division facts in 3 minutes. Then: 'A box holds 9 eggs. How many in 7 boxes?' Mark together and note any facts to practise.
days.en: Dictation: '"Take your medicine," said the doctor.' and '"Is this the particular musician?" asked the girl.' Check inverted commas, commas and question marks.

weeks.title: The 7, 11 and 12 times tables; multiplying by 0 and 1

spell.rule: Homophones: grate/great, groan/grown, heel/heal/he'll, knot/not, mail/male

weeks.read: A collection of poems that are fun to perform aloud, including some with conversations or two voices.

days.ma: 7 times table: build it from known facts (7 × 2 = 14, 7 × 5 = 35, so 7 × 7 = 35 + 14 = 49). Write it out, then chant it, then answer 10 mixed questions with division too.
days.en: Choose a poem with two voices or dialogue to perform. Read it aloud together, deciding who says which lines and how loudly, quickly or slowly each part should be read.

days.ma: 11 and 12 times tables: spot patterns (11 × 4 = 44; 12 × n = 10 × n + 2 × n). Work out 12 × 7 as 70 + 14. Write both tables, then do 10 mixed questions.
days.en: Write a short scene with two characters arguing about who will carry a heavy bag. Use direct speech with new speakers on new lines, with correct inverted commas, commas and question marks.

days.ma: Multiplying by 0 and 1, dividing by 1: try 0 × 8, 8 × 1, 8 ÷ 1, 0 × 1000, 245 × 1. Talk about why any number times 0 is 0 and times 1 stays the same. Make up a silly word problem for each.
days.en: Homophones: write grate/great, groan/grown, heel/heal/he'll, knot/not and mail/male on cards. Play snap with sentence cards, then write two sentences using two homophones each.

days.ma: Times table bingo: draw a 3 × 3 grid with answers from the 7, 11 and 12 tables; call questions (7 × 8, 12 × 6, 11 × 9 …) and cross off. Learn the word group and write 'Our group knows the 12s.'
days.en: Rehearse the poem from Monday. Practise pauses, volume and actions. Then read your own dialogue scene aloud as a little play, using expression to show how each character feels.

days.ma: Friday check: 15 mixed questions from the 7, 11 and 12 tables (including division) in 3 minutes, plus 9 × 0, 1 × 63, 56 ÷ 1. Mark and note any facts to practise next week.
days.en: Perform the poem to the family. Then dictation: '"That knot is great!" said the group leader.' Check the inverted commas and the homophone spellings.

weeks.title: Factor pairs and multiplying three numbers

spell.rule: Possessive apostrophes with plural nouns: for plurals ending in s, add the apostrophe after the s (the girls' coats, the horses' field); for irregular plurals, add 's (children's, men's, women's, mice's)

weeks.read: A story told from more than one character's point of view, or a story your child chooses with lots of characters.

days.ma: Factor pairs: find all the pairs of numbers that multiply to make 24 by arranging 24 buttons or pasta pieces into rectangles (1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8, 4 × 6). Repeat for 36 and 30.
days.en: Possessive apostrophes: write 'the girl's bag' (one girl) and 'the girls' bags' (many girls). Then irregular plurals: 'the children's coats', 'the women's shoes'. Make a table with singular, plural, singular possessive and plural possessive.

days.ma: Multiply three numbers: 2 × 7 × 5. Show that doing 2 × 5 first (10 × 7 = 70) is easier. Try 4 × 9 × 5, 3 × 2 × 8 and 6 × 5 × 2, choosing the easiest order each time.
days.en: Apostrophe hunt: in a reading book, find five possessive apostrophes. Decide if each is one owner or many owners and how you can tell. Then find two apostrophes for missing letters (contractions) to compare.

days.ma: Derived facts: if 6 × 7 = 42, what is 60 × 7? 6 × 70? 42 ÷ 7? 420 ÷ 6? Make a 'fact web' around 8 × 9 = 72 with as many related facts as you can.
days.en: Edit: re-read the dialogue scene from last week. Add a possessive apostrophe sentence (the twins' bikes, the women's hats) and check every piece of direct speech is punctuated correctly.

days.ma: Factor games: say a number from the times tables (48, 56, 72); your child finds all the factor pairs. Then quick tables round: 12 questions on the 6s, 7s and 9s.
days.en: Spelling: write the plural possessives of dog, horse, child, man, woman and mouse in phrases (the dogs' bowls, the children's toys). Learn woman/women and say what changes.

days.ma: Friday check: list all factor pairs of 20 and 18. Calculate 5 × 3 × 4 and 2 × 9 × 5. If 7 × 8 = 56, what is 70 × 8? Answer 6 × 0 and 72 ÷ 1. Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'The women's coats were in the girls' bedroom.' and 'The children's dog lost its bone.' Check each apostrophe and talk about why its has none.

weeks.title: Consolidation: calculation, area and times tables

spell.rule: Revise this half term: -tion, -sion, -ssion, -cian, homophones and plural possessive apostrophes

weeks.read: A short winter or festive story or poem collection to share before the holiday.

days.ma: Calculation mix: 4526 + 2789 and 7004 – 3658, each with an estimate and inverse check. Then the two-step problem: 'A charity raises £2350 in one month and £1785 in the next. They need £5000. How much more?'
days.en: Spelling round-up: read 10 words (invention, extension, permission, musician, possession, mention, medicine, particular, group, women). Your child writes them; tick and practise any slips.

days.ma: Times tables relay: 20 mixed questions on all tables to 12 × 12, with a 3-minute target. Then list the factor pairs of 60 and calculate 4 × 7 × 5.
days.en: Punctuation recap: write a sentence with a fronted adverbial and comma, a line of direct speech, and a phrase with a plural possessive apostrophe. Check them together.

days.ma: Area: draw a floor plan of a bedroom on squared paper (each square is 1 square metre) with a bed and a desk. Find the area of the whole room and of the free floor space.
days.en: Book chat: each person chooses their favourite character met this term and argues why. Take turns and ask one follow-up question each.

days.ma: Problem day: 'A cinema has 12 rows of 9 seats. 87 tickets are sold. How many seats are empty?' Plan, estimate, solve and check. Then make up a similar problem for a grown-up.
days.en: Handwriting: copy a short winter poem in best joined handwriting, keeping letters the same size and lines well spaced. Read it aloud with expression.

days.ma: Term check: 12 mixed questions, e.g. 3742 + 1569; 6000 – 2874; area of an L-shape; 9 × 7; 84 ÷ 12; factor pairs of 16; 3 × 2 × 10. Celebrate progress and note facts to keep practising over the holiday.
days.en: Dictation: '"Consider the women's choice," said the magician.' and 'We were given permission to see the girls' invention.' Proof-read for punctuation and spelling.

weeks.title: Multiplying 2-digit numbers by 1-digit numbers

spell.rule: Prefixes inter- (between or among) and sub- (under or below): interact, international, intercity; subheading, submarine, submerge, subdivide

weeks.read: Leaflets, posters and adverts collected from around the home, the library or a museum, to read as persuasive texts.

days.ma: Grid method: 34 × 6 is 30 × 6 + 4 × 6 = 180 + 24 = 204. Draw the grid, then try 47 × 3 and 58 × 4. Talk about how splitting the tens and ones makes it easier (the distributive law).
days.en: Start a persuasive writing unit: read two leaflets or adverts together. Find persuasive tricks: questions to the reader, exciting adjectives, facts and numbers, and 'you' language. List them.

days.ma: Formal written layout: show 34 × 6 in columns, multiplying the ones first (4 × 6 = 24, write 4, carry 2) then the tens (3 × 6 = 18, plus 2 = 20). Compare with the grid answer, then try 63 × 7.
days.en: Retrieve facts: from a leaflet, find the place, opening times, price and three reasons to visit. Record them in a table with headings.

days.ma: Real-life multiplying: 'A packet of biscuits costs 76p. How much for 5 packets?' 'One page has 28 lines. How many lines on 6 pages?' Estimate first (80p × 5), then use the column method.
days.en: Spelling: add inter- or sub- to national, city, act, heading, marine and merge. Use the meaning of the prefix to explain each word. Learn interest and sentence.

days.ma: Tables warm-up: 3 minutes of 7s and 8s. Then compare 3 × 46 and 46 × 3 – same answer? Calculate 26 × 4 three ways: grid, columns, and doubling twice.
days.en: Plan your own leaflet persuading families to visit a local park or a pretend attraction. Note headings, sub-headings, persuasive phrases and three facts. Use the words 'heading' and 'sub-heading' when planning.

days.ma: Friday check: 23 × 4; 56 × 3; 79 × 6; 'Seven boxes each hold 45 pencils. How many pencils?' Show one answer using the grid and one using columns. Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'The submarine was of great interest to international visitors.' and 'Write a sentence with a subheading.' Check capitals and the spellings of interest and sentence.

weeks.title: Multiplying 3-digit numbers and dividing by 1-digit numbers

spell.rule: Prefixes super- (above or more than), anti- (against) and auto- (self): supermarket, superstar, superhero; antiseptic, anticlockwise, antisocial; autobiography, autograph, automatic

weeks.read: A persuasive book review or a page of 'top ten' recommendations from a children's magazine or library display.

days.ma: 3-digit by 1-digit: 243 × 4 in columns (ones, then tens, then hundreds, carrying as needed). Then 316 × 5 and 427 × 6. Estimate each first (240 × 4 is about 1000).
days.en: Draft the leaflet: write a catchy heading, a question to hook the reader ('Looking for a great day out?') and a first section under a sub-heading using expanded noun phrases.

days.ma: Dividing using known facts: 84 ÷ 4 – split into 80 ÷ 4 and 4 ÷ 4 = 20 + 1 = 21. Try 96 ÷ 3, 72 ÷ 6 and 65 ÷ 5. Check each answer by multiplying.
days.en: Draft two more sections. Use conjunctions and adverbials of time and cause ('because', 'so', 'as soon as you arrive'), and present perfect phrases such as 'Thousands of families have enjoyed …'.

days.ma: Dividing with remainders: share 47 pasta pieces among 3 bowls. Record 47 ÷ 3 = 15 r 2. Try 59 ÷ 4 and 85 ÷ 6. Talk about what the remainder means in each story.
days.en: Spelling: add super-, anti- or auto- to market, star, clockwise, septic, graph and biography. Explain the meaning of each prefix. Learn continue and write 'Continue the superhero's story.'

days.ma: Mental strategies: 6 × 25 (double 3 × 25), 4 × 125, 180 ÷ 6 (using 18 ÷ 6), 7 × 40 (7 × 4 × 10). Then a round of 12s and 11s facts.
days.en: Read the leaflet draft aloud and check every sentence. Correct any non-standard English, then add a final section 'Why you must visit' with three bullet points.

days.ma: Friday check: 214 × 3; 352 × 6; 96 ÷ 4; 78 ÷ 5 (with remainder); 'A car travels 128 miles each day for 5 days. How far altogether?' Mark together and check one by the inverse.
days.en: Dictation: 'Turn the dial anticlockwise and continue.' and 'The superstar signed an autograph.' Check capitals, full stops and the spellings of continue and anticlockwise.

weeks.title: Scaling and correspondence problems

spell.rule: The suffix -ation turns verbs into nouns (inform → information, adore → adoration, sense → sensation, prepare → preparation, admire → admiration)

weeks.read: A playscript or a book of short plays to read aloud together, getting ready for next week.

days.ma: Scaling: 'A sunflower is 4 times as tall as a 35 cm seedling. How tall is it?' 'A dog weighs 6 times as much as a 12 kg puppy.' Draw bar models to show 'times as many' before calculating.
days.en: Evaluate the leaflet: read it with a grown-up as if you were a visitor. Which part is most persuasive? Which part is boring? Make two improvements to vocabulary.

days.ma: Correspondence: 'You have 4 T-shirts and 3 pairs of shorts. How many different outfits?' Use real clothes or drawings to list them systematically (12). Then try 5 sandwich fillings and 3 breads.
days.en: Proof-read the leaflet line by line with a ruler under each line. Check spellings with a dictionary, and check capital letters in headings and full stops in sentences.

days.ma: Recipe scaling: take a simple recipe for 2 people. Multiply every ingredient to feed 6 people, then 8. Use the written method for any tricky ones (e.g. 125 g × 3).
days.en: Spelling: add -ation to inform, adore, sense, prepare and admire (drop e where needed). Learn exercise and write 'Preparation and exercise give you a great sensation.'

days.ma: Mixed problem: 'Each child in a class of 28 needs 3 pencils and 2 rubbers. How many items altogether?' Solve two different ways (28 × 5 or 28 × 3 + 28 × 2) and compare.
days.en: Word families: from 'inform' build information, informative, informed and misinform. Do the same for 'prepare' and 'sign' (signal, signature). Talk about how the root keeps its meaning.

days.ma: Friday check: 3 times as heavy as 27 kg; 4 hats and 3 scarves – how many combinations?; 167 × 4; 'Adult tickets cost £8 and child tickets £5. How much for 9 adults and 3 children?' Mark together.
days.en: Present the finished leaflet by reading it aloud to the family with a persuasive voice. Then dictation: 'The information about exercise caused a sensation.'

weeks.title: Length: kilometres, metres, centimetres and millimetres

spell.rule: Homophones: main/mane, meat/meet, medal/meddle, missed/mist, peace/piece

weeks.read: A playscript read aloud together with each person taking parts; look at how it is set out differently from a story.

days.ma: Units of length: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm. Measure your hand span in cm and mm, the table in cm and m, and talk about the distance to a local shop in km and m. Convert 3 km to metres, 6000 m to kilometres and 4 m 35 cm to centimetres.
days.en: Read a playscript together. Find the character list, stage directions (often in brackets or italics) and the speaker's name before each line. Talk about how this differs from direct speech in a story.

days.ma: Estimate then measure: estimate the length of 5 objects (spoon, door height, book width, shoe, pencil), measure each, and record the difference between estimate and measurement in cm or mm.
days.en: Turn speech into script: take a short conversation from a story (with inverted commas) and rewrite it as a playscript. Then turn a short playscript back into story dialogue with correct punctuation.

days.ma: Conversions: 4 m = __ cm; 650 cm = __ m __ cm; 7 cm 3 mm = __ mm; 2000 m = __ km. Then order 1 m 5 cm, 150 cm, 1050 mm and 2 m.
days.en: Homophones: write main/mane, meat/meet, medal/meddle, missed/mist and peace/piece on cards. Read sentences and hold up the correct spelling. Learn earth and write a sentence about the Earth.

days.ma: Walk and measure: count your steps for 10 metres (measure with a tape or a ruler and string), then estimate how many steps make 1 km (multiply). Calculate the total distance of a short walk in metres.
days.en: Prepare the playscript for performance: mark where voices should be loud, quiet, fast or slow, and add one action for each character.

days.ma: Friday check: 5 km = __ m; 320 cm = __ m __ cm; 45 mm = __ cm __ mm; which is longer, 1 m 9 cm or 190 cm? A ribbon is 2 m long; 75 cm is cut off – how much is left? Mark together.
days.en: Perform the playscript to the family. Then dictation: '"Did you see the mist over the earth?" asked the farmer.' Check inverted commas and the homophone mist.

weeks.title: Perimeter of rectangles and rectilinear shapes

spell.rule: Words ending -ture and -sure (creature, furniture, adventure, temperature; measure, treasure, enclosure, pressure)

weeks.read: A second playscript, or a story your child adapts into a playscript, read aloud with expression.

days.ma: Perimeter is the distance all the way round a shape. Measure the perimeter of a book, a placemat and a door in cm or m, adding all sides. Record in a table.
days.en: Write a short playscript scene (about 10 lines) based on a familiar fairy tale but set somewhere unexpected. Include a character list, setting, stage directions in brackets and speakers' names.

days.ma: Rectangle shortcuts: for a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm, the perimeter is 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 or (8 + 5) × 2 = 26 cm. Try a 12 m by 7 m garden and a 25 cm square (4 × 25).
days.en: Continue the playscript: add a problem and a twist, with stage directions to show how characters move and feel (e.g. '(nervously, backing away)').

days.ma: Rectilinear shapes: draw an L-shape on squared paper and find its perimeter. Some side lengths are missing – work them out from the others. Then draw your own and swap.
days.en: Spelling: add -ture or -sure to make creature, furniture, adventure, measure, treasure and enclosure. Learn pressure and natural (from nature) with look–say–cover–write–check.

days.ma: Make it: build shapes with an area of 12 squares on squared paper and find the perimeter of each. Which has the longest perimeter? Then a 3-minute round of 7s and 12s tables.
days.en: Handwriting: write out the finished playscript neatly, setting it out with speakers' names on the left and stage directions in brackets.

days.ma: Friday check: perimeter of a 9 cm by 4 cm rectangle; a square with sides of 15 m; an L-shape you draw with two missing sides; convert a 3 m perimeter into cm. Mark together.
days.en: Perform the playscript, controlling tone and volume so the audience can follow. Then dictation: 'There was great pressure to find the natural treasure.'

weeks.title: Consolidation: multiplication, length and perimeter

spell.rule: Revise this half term: inter-/sub-, super-/anti-/auto-, -ation, homophones, -ture/-sure

weeks.read: Your child's choice of book – fiction, poetry or fact – for the half-term break.

days.ma: Multiplication relay: 36 × 4, 248 × 3, 507 × 6 (with estimates). Then 'A plant is 5 times as tall as a 24 cm seedling. How tall is it in metres and centimetres?'
days.en: Spelling round-up: read 10 words (international, submarine, superstar, autograph, information, interest, continue, exercise, pressure, natural). Your child writes them; tick and practise any slips.

days.ma: Perimeter and length: find the perimeter of a 1 m 20 cm by 80 cm table in cm, then in m and cm. Convert 2400 m to km and m. Then 20 mixed tables questions in 3 minutes.
days.en: Grammar recap: name and use a fronted adverbial, an expanded noun phrase, a conjunction and the present perfect. Make each into a sentence about a playground. Use the word grammar in a sentence.

days.ma: Problem: 'A rectangular garden is 14 m by 9 m. Fencing costs £6 per metre. How much for the whole perimeter?' Solve step by step and check.
days.en: Book chat: talk about the persuasive leaflet and the playscript. Which was more fun to write and why? Listen and respond to each other.

days.ma: Factor pairs and mental: factor pairs of 48 and 72; 5 × 9 × 2; 600 ÷ 3; 25 × 8. Then make up a scaling problem for a grown-up to solve.
days.en: Proof-read a piece of writing from this half term. Use a dictionary to check at least three spellings and correct any missing commas after fronted adverbials.

days.ma: Half-term check: 12 mixed questions, e.g. 63 × 7; 418 × 5; 84 ÷ 7; 3 km in m; perimeter of a 7 cm square; 6 × 12; factor pairs of 32; 4 outfits from 2 tops and 2 skirts. Celebrate progress.
days.en: Dictation: 'At the international match, the superstar signed autographs.' and '"Check your grammar," said the teacher.' Then a neat copy in best handwriting.

weeks.title: Equivalent fractions

spell.rule: Adding vowel suffixes (-ing, -ed, -er) to words of more than one syllable: double the last consonant if the last syllable is stressed (forget → forgetting, begin → beginning, prefer → preferred) but not if it isn't (garden → gardening, limit → limited)

weeks.read: An adventure story with a journey or a quest, read independently with a chapter shared aloud each evening.

days.ma: Fold paper strips into halves, quarters and eighths, and another set into thirds and sixths. Line them up to show 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8 and 1/3 = 2/6. Record each family of equivalent fractions.
days.en: Start an adventure story unit. Read the opening chapter and talk about how the writer hooks you in: a mystery, an exciting event, a strong character? Note three words or phrases that grab your interest.

days.ma: Draw a fraction wall on squared paper with rows for 1, halves, thirds, quarters, fifths, sixths, eighths, tenths and twelfths. Find as many equivalents as you can for 1/2, 1/3 and 3/4.
days.en: Spelling: add -ing and -ed to forget, begin, prefer, garden, limit and visit, deciding each time whether to double the last letter. Say each word aloud to hear where the stress is. Learn forward(s).

days.ma: Equivalent fractions by multiplying: 1/4 = 2/8 because top and bottom are both doubled. Use times tables to find three more fractions equal to 2/3 (4/6, 6/9, 8/12) and 3/5.
days.en: Read on and infer: find a moment where a character is scared or excited. Explain how you know, quoting the text. Predict what they will do next and why.

days.ma: Pizza equivalents: draw two circles. Cut one into 4 slices and shade 2; cut the other into 8 and shade 4. Talk about why the shaded parts are the same. Then a 3-minute round of 6s, 7s and 9s tables.
days.en: Exception words: list words from the adventure book that have unusual spellings (e.g. island, through, enough, journey). Note where the tricky part is and learn three of them.

days.ma: Friday check: complete 1/2 = __/8; 3/4 = 9/__; 2/5 = __/10. Circle the fraction that is not equal to the others: 2/6, 1/3, 3/9, 3/6. Draw a diagram to show 2/3 = 4/6. Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'Beginning the journey, the travellers went forward.' and 'Have you forgotten the map?' Check the comma, question mark and the doubled consonants.

weeks.title: Adding and subtracting fractions with the same denominator

spell.rule: The k sound spelt ch (scheme, chorus, chemist, echo, character, stomach) and the sh sound spelt ch, from French (chef, machine, brochure, chalet, parachute)

weeks.read: Carry on with the adventure story; look out for how chapters start and end with a cliffhanger.

days.ma: Use the paper strips: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8. Talk about why the denominator stays the same. Then try 3/10 + 4/10, 5/12 + 6/12 and 7/9 – 4/9 using drawings.
days.en: Plan your own adventure story: draw a map of the journey with four stages (setting off, a problem, a twist, the ending). Note the main character, their goal and something that stands in their way.

days.ma: Fractions greater than one: 5/6 + 4/6 = 9/6, which is 1 and 3/6. Show it with two drawn bars split into sixths. Try 7/8 + 3/8 and 4/5 + 4/5.
days.en: Paragraph plan: split the plan into five paragraphs and write the topic of each (setting, meeting the problem, the struggle, the twist, the resolution). Talk about the adverbial that could start each one.

days.ma: Subtracting from a whole: 1 – 3/8 = 8/8 – 3/8 = 5/8. Try 1 – 2/5 and 2 – 5/6. Then a story problem: 'A cake is cut into 12 slices. 5/12 are eaten at lunch and 4/12 at tea. What fraction is left?'
days.en: Spelling: sort scheme, chorus, chemist, echo, character, chef, machine, brochure and parachute by the sound of ch. Learn experience and experiment.

days.ma: Make your own fraction sums: roll a dice twice to make the numerators of two twelfths (e.g. 4/12 + 5/12). Add them and say whether the answer is more or less than a whole. Then 2 minutes of 11s and 12s.
days.en: Roots and meanings: find words that share a root, like character/characterise, chemist/chemistry, experience/inexperienced. Use a dictionary to check meanings.

days.ma: Friday check: 3/7 + 2/7; 5/9 – 1/9; 7/10 + 6/10 (write as a mixed number); 1 – 4/11; 'A tank is 3/8 full. 4/8 more is added. How full is it now?' Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'The chef's experiment went wrong.' and 'The character had experience of using a parachute.' Check the apostrophe and the ch words.

weeks.title: Fractions of amounts

spell.rule: Words ending -gue and -que, from French (league, tongue, rogue, catalogue; antique, unique, cheque, plaque)

weeks.read: An adventure story by a different writer, to compare how each one builds excitement.

days.ma: Unit fractions of amounts: find 1/4 of 20 buttons by sharing into 4 groups. Then 1/3 of 18, 1/5 of 35 and 1/8 of 48, using division facts.
days.en: Draft the first two paragraphs of the adventure story. Start with a fronted adverbial and introduce the main character with an expanded noun phrase. Include one line of direct speech.

days.ma: Non-unit fractions: 3/4 of 20 is 3 lots of 1/4 of 20 = 3 × 5 = 15. Draw a bar model. Try 2/3 of 24, 3/5 of 40 and 5/8 of 64.
days.en: Draft the middle paragraphs where the problem gets worse. Use direct speech to show the characters' feelings, starting a new line for each new speaker and punctuating it correctly.

days.ma: Kitchen fractions: 'A bag of 30 sweets – I eat 2/5. How many is that?' Use real objects (pasta, coins, raisins) to check. Then find 3/10 of 50p and 3/4 of 1 hour in minutes.
days.en: Spelling: read league, tongue, rogue, catalogue, antique, unique, cheque and plaque. Learn extreme. Then write the words with the tricky endings from memory.

days.ma: Working backwards: 'A quarter of a number is 7. What is the number?' (28). Draw bars to solve 1/5 of a number is 9 and 2/3 of a number is 12. Then a quick 7s and 8s tables round.
days.en: Draft the ending: solve the problem and show how the character has changed. Add a paragraph with a time adverbial such as 'At long last,'.

days.ma: Friday check: 1/6 of 42; 3/4 of 32; 2/5 of 45; 7/10 of 100; 'A class has 28 children. 3/4 have a pet. How many have no pet?' Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: '"This antique map is unique!" gasped the explorer.' and 'The extreme cold froze her tongue.' Check inverted commas and the -que and -gue spellings.

weeks.title: Tenths and hundredths

spell.rule: Homophones: plain/plane, rain/rein/reign, scene/seen, weather/whether, whose/who's

weeks.read: A short story collection; read one story each day and decide which ending is strongest.

days.ma: Hundredths: draw a 10 by 10 square on squared paper (100 small squares). Shade 1 column – that is 1/10 or 10/100. Shade 1 small square – that is 1/100. Shade 37 squares and write 37/100 and 0.37.
days.en: Edit the adventure story: read it aloud. Does every paragraph have one main idea? Are there places where 'he' or 'she' is confusing? Replace unclear pronouns with nouns and repeated nouns with pronouns.

days.ma: Tenths divided by 10 make hundredths: shade 1/10 of the hundred square, then split that column into 10 – each part is 1/100. Count up in hundredths from 0.01 to 0.20 and back again.
days.en: Improve vocabulary: find five ordinary verbs or adjectives in your story and swap them for stronger ones (went → crept, big → towering). Explain why each new word is better.

days.ma: Decimal place value: write 0.6, 0.06, 0.65 and 1.45 on a place value chart with columns ones, tenths and hundredths. Say what each digit is worth. Match each to a fraction (65/100 …).
days.en: Homophones: write sentences for plain/plane, rain/rein/reign, scene/seen, weather/whether and whose/who's with a gap; your child chooses the correct word. Learn strange.

days.ma: Money as hundredths: £1 = 100p, so 1p = £0.01. Write 7p, 45p, £1.23 and £3.05 using the pound sign and decimal point. Then count up in steps of 0.05 from 0 to 1.
days.en: Grammar: find the present perfect in your story or add some ('The storm has stopped.'). Talk about how it differs from 'The storm stopped.'

days.ma: Friday check: write 3/10 and 47/100 as decimals; write 0.09 as a fraction; what is the 4 worth in 2.43? Count on 5 hundredths from 0.18. Shade 0.7 on a hundred square. Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'Whose strange plane is that?' and 'Who's seen the rain in the scene?' Check question marks, the apostrophe in who's and the spelling of strange.

weeks.title: Dividing by 10 and 100; decimals for quarters and halves

spell.rule: The sh sound spelt -tion, -sion, -ssion or -cian: choosing the right ending from the root word (action, tension, discussion, magician)

weeks.read: A children's newspaper or news website article read together (with an adult choosing a suitable story).

days.ma: Divide by 10 on a place value chart: 7 ÷ 10 = 0.7 (digits move one place right). Then 34 ÷ 10 = 3.4 and 34 ÷ 100 = 0.34. Use counters to show the digits moving and say the value of each digit in the answer.
days.en: Start a news report unit. Read a news article together and find the headline, the opening paragraph that answers who, what, where, when and why, quotations, and a photo with a caption.

days.ma: Quarters and halves: 1/2 = 50/100 = 0.5, 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25 and 3/4 = 75/100 = 0.75. Show each on a hundred square and on a 0 to 1 number line. Link to 50p, 25p and 75p.
days.en: Retrieve facts: from the article, make a table with who, what, where, when and why. Then summarise the main idea in one sentence of no more than 20 words.

days.ma: Divide by 100: 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05, 47 ÷ 100 = 0.47, 80 ÷ 100 = 0.8. Then convert lengths: 47 cm = 0.47 m and 5 cm = 0.05 m. Measure three objects in cm and write them in metres.
days.en: Plan a news report about a recent event at home or school (a new pet, a sports day, an exciting discovery in the garden). Write a headline, the who/what/where/when/why, and an interview quotation.

days.ma: Matching game: make cards for 1/2, 0.5, 50/100, 1/4, 0.25, 25/100, 3/4, 0.75, 75/100, 3/10, 0.3, 30/100. Turn them face down and play pairs. Then 2 minutes of mixed tables.
days.en: Draft the report: an opening paragraph with the key facts, then a paragraph with more detail, a quotation in inverted commas, and a closing sentence. Use the past tense and standard English.

days.ma: Friday check: 6 ÷ 10; 58 ÷ 10; 58 ÷ 100; write 3/4 and 1/4 as decimals; what is 0.5 as a fraction? 'A ribbon is 9 cm. Write its length in metres.' Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'In a recent discussion, the magician explained his action.' and '"I was full of tension," said the witness.' Check inverted commas and the sh endings.

weeks.title: Consolidation: fractions and decimals

spell.rule: Revise this half term: doubling before vowel suffixes, ch words, -gue/-que, homophones and -tion/-sion/-ssion/-cian

weeks.read: Re-read the best adventure story from this half term and choose a chapter to read aloud.

days.ma: Fraction review: find three fractions equivalent to 3/4; 4/9 + 3/9; 1 – 5/12; 2/3 of 27. Draw a diagram for each and check together.
days.en: Spelling round-up: read 10 words (beginning, preferred, character, machine, unique, tongue, whose, strange, experiment, recent). Your child writes them; tick and practise any slips.

days.ma: Decimal review: write 0.7, 0.07 and 0.75 as fractions; divide 9, 36 and 70 by 10 and by 100; count back in hundredths from 0.25 to 0.15.
days.en: Proof-read the news report from last week. Check inverted commas, commas after fronted adverbials and spellings. Use a dictionary for two words and publish a neat copy.

days.ma: Problem day: 'A recipe needs 3/4 of a 400 g bag of flour. How much is that?' and 'A tower of 10 identical blocks is 37 cm tall. How tall is one block?' (3.7 cm).
days.en: Read the news report aloud like a newsreader, using a clear voice and pausing at full stops and commas. Record it if you can and listen back.

days.ma: Matching relay: call out a fraction (1/4, 3/10, 47/100, 1/2); your child writes the decimal and shades a hundred square. Then 20 mixed tables questions to increase speed.
days.en: Book chat: compare the two adventure stories from this half term. Which hero was braver? Which beginning was most gripping? Take turns and build on what the other person says.

days.ma: Half-term check: 12 mixed questions, e.g. 2/5 = __/10; 5/8 + 2/8; 3/4 of 24; 0.3 as a fraction; 27 ÷ 10; 3/4 as a decimal; 'Which is greater, 0.6 or 0.06?'. Celebrate and note what to revisit.
days.en: Dictation: '"We must increase our speed," whispered the character.' and 'Whose plane landed in the plain?' Then copy one sentence in best joined handwriting.

weeks.title: Comparing, ordering and rounding decimals

spell.rule: Adding -ly to make adverbs, including words ending -le (gentle → gently), -ic (basic → basically) and y (happy → happily), and exceptions (true → truly, full → fully)

weeks.read: A poetry anthology with different forms – free verse, narrative poems, shape poems and poems that rhyme.

days.ma: Compare decimals: which is greater, 0.4 or 0.37? Shade both on hundred squares (0.4 = 0.40). Then order 2.3, 2.03, 3.2 and 2.32 using a place value chart. Use < and >.
days.en: Read a free verse poem and a narrative poem (one that tells a story). Talk about how they are different: rhyme, rhythm, line length and story. Which do you prefer and why?

days.ma: Round to the nearest whole number: draw a line from 4 to 5 marked in tenths. Mark 4.3 and 4.8 and decide which whole number each is nearer. Agree that 4.5 rounds up. Round 6.2, 9.5 and 12.7.
days.en: Discuss favourite phrases: choose a poem and pick three phrases that create a picture in your mind. Explain what each makes you imagine and how the poet chose the words.

days.ma: Kitchen decimals: read the weights on food packets in kg (e.g. 1.5 kg, 0.75 kg) or drinks in litres. Order them, then round each to the nearest whole kg or litre.
days.en: Spelling: add -ly to gentle, simple, basic, dramatic, happy, true and full. Sort them by what changed. Learn probably and accidentally, noticing the -ally ending.

days.ma: Decimal race: write 10 decimals with two places on scraps (e.g. 3.45, 3.54, 4.35, 0.99). Race to put them in order. Then 3 minutes of 7s, 8s and 12s tables.
days.en: Word roots: look for prefixes and suffixes in a poem (re-, un-, -ful, -ly, -ness). Take a root word such as 'hope' and build as many words as you can (hopeful, hopeless, hopefully, hopelessness).

days.ma: Friday check: put <, > or = between 0.5 and 0.50, 1.09 and 1.9, 3.6 and 3.06; order 0.7, 0.07, 0.17, 0.71; round 5.4, 7.5 and 19.9 to the nearest whole number. Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'She probably fell over accidentally.' and 'Gently, the poet basically read the poem.' Check the commas and the -ly spellings.

weeks.title: Money: pounds and pence

spell.rule: Homophones: fair/fare, brake/break, ball/bawl, heard/herd, who's/whose and the tricky trio there/their/they're

weeks.read: Poems about animals or nature, chosen to give ideas for your own poem this week.

days.ma: Price list: write prices from a receipt or a pretend café menu (e.g. £2.45, £1.80, 95p). Convert pence to pounds and pounds to pence. Order the prices from cheapest to dearest.
days.en: Choose a form for your own poem (free verse or a short narrative poem about a naughty animal). Read one example together and note how it is set out on the page.

days.ma: Adding money: 'A sandwich costs £2.75 and a drink £1.45. What is the total?' Add pounds and pence separately or in columns. Then find the change from £5. Count it out with real coins if you have them.
days.en: Draft the poem: aim for 8–12 lines. Use expanded noun phrases, powerful verbs and one simile ('as quick as …'). Don't worry about rhyme – focus on pictures in words.

days.ma: Estimating money: estimate the total of five items from a shopping list by rounding each to the nearest pound. Then calculate accurately and compare. Was the estimate close?
days.en: Homophones: write sentences with gaps for fair/fare, brake/break, heard/herd and there/their/they're. Your child fills them in. Learn naughty and write 'The naughty dog ate their dinner.'

days.ma: Money problems with fractions: 'A £12 book is reduced by 1/4. What is the new price?' 'A bag of 6 apples costs £1.80. How much for one?' Then 2 minutes of mixed tables.
days.en: Rehearse the poem: decide where to pause, which words to stress and whether to speed up or slow down. Mark these on your copy.

days.ma: Friday check: £3.45 + £2.70; change from £10 for £6.85; write 405p in pounds; 'Three cinema tickets cost £7.50 each. What is the total?'; 1/2 of £4.60. Mark together.
days.en: Perform your poem to the family with expression. Then dictation: 'The naughty herd broke the fence near the fair.'

weeks.title: Time: 12-hour and 24-hour clocks

spell.rule: The short i sound spelt y (myth, gym, mystery, pyramid, Egypt) and the u sound spelt ou (young, touch, double, trouble, country)

weeks.read: Instruction texts: recipes, craft guides or game rules, read to see how they are organised.

days.ma: Read analogue clocks with Roman numerals and with numbers. Then convert times to digital: 'twenty to four' = 3:40. Make a paper clock face and set times for your partner to read.
days.en: Start an instructions unit. Read a recipe or game rules together. Find the title, 'You will need' list, numbered steps, bossy verbs (commands) and time words. Make a checklist of features.

days.ma: 24-hour clock: draw a timeline from midnight to midnight with both 12-hour and 24-hour times. Convert 3:15 p.m. to 15:15, 9:40 p.m. to 21:40 and 07:05 to 7:05 a.m.
days.en: Plan instructions for something you can really do at home, such as making mashed potatoes or a paper aeroplane. Do it first and note each step and the equipment.

days.ma: Timetable hunt: look at a bus or train timetable (printed or online) or make a pretend one. Find a journey, convert times to 12-hour, and work out how long the journey takes.
days.en: Draft the instructions: numbered steps that start with commanding verbs ('Peel', 'Fold'), adverbials of time ('After 5 minutes,'), and a tip box. Use standard English throughout.

days.ma: Household clocks: compare the time on the oven, a phone and a wall clock. Are they 12-hour or 24-hour? Write each time both ways. Then a quick round of 6s and 9s tables.
days.en: Spelling: read myth, gym, mystery, pyramid, Egypt, young, touch, double and trouble. Learn potatoes and talk about why it adds -es. Spot exception words like 'country' with ou making a u sound.

days.ma: Friday check: write 4:25 p.m. in 24-hour time; write 19:50 as a 12-hour time; draw hands for 10:35 on a clock face with Roman numerals; read XI on a clock. Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'First, boil the potatoes for twenty minutes.' and 'Is the gym open at 17:00?' Check commas, question mark and the spelling of potatoes.

weeks.title: Converting units of time

spell.rule: Word families from the same root (solve, solution, dissolve; sign, signal, signature; know, knowledge, acknowledge; strong, strength, strengthen)

weeks.read: A fact book with timelines (history, inventions or space) to practise reading dates and durations.

days.ma: Time facts: 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour, 24 hours = 1 day, 7 days = 1 week, 12 months = 1 year. Make a poster. Then convert 3 hours to minutes and 120 seconds to minutes.
days.en: Finish the instructions draft from last week. Add a short introduction ('Have you ever wanted to …?') and a closing sentence. Read it aloud to check every step is in the right order.

days.ma: Converting problems: 'How many days in 6 weeks?' 'How many months in 4 years?' 'A film lasts 135 minutes. How many hours and minutes?' Use tables facts and show working.
days.en: Evaluate: a grown-up follows the instructions exactly as written (even if silly). Did it work? Which steps need to be clearer? Edit together.

days.ma: Your age in time: how old are you in years and months? In weeks (about)? In days (about)? Use multiplication to work it out, rounding where sensible.
days.en: Spelling: build word families from solve, sign, know and strong. Learn knowledge and strength. Use a dictionary to check two words you are not sure about.

days.ma: Timer challenge: how many star jumps in 1 minute? In 30 seconds? Predict how many in 5 minutes using multiplication. Then convert 300 seconds to minutes.
days.en: Grammar words: in your instructions, find and label a command, a fronted adverbial, a determiner, a preposition and a pronoun. Explain each choice using the correct terms.

days.ma: Friday check: 5 minutes = __ seconds; 4 weeks = __ days; 48 months = __ years; 2 hours 15 minutes = __ minutes; 'School starts at 08:45 and lunch is 3 hours 30 minutes later. What time is lunch?'. Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: '"Knowledge is strength," said the wise woman.' and 'Stir the solution until it dissolves.' Check the inverted commas and the spellings of knowledge and strength.

weeks.title: Bar charts, tables and time graphs

spell.rule: Prefixes dis-, mis-, un- and re- reviewed with longer words (disappointment, misunderstand, unbelievable, reconsider)

weeks.read: A fact book with charts and graphs, or a letter collection, to see how letters are set out.

days.ma: Family survey: ask everyone their favourite fruit. Record in a tally chart, then draw a bar chart with a labelled scale going up in 2s. Talk about which is most and least popular.
days.en: Read a letter (a real postcard or a letter from a book). Find the address, date, greeting, paragraphs and sign-off. Talk about the difference between a friendly and a formal letter.

days.ma: Time graph: measure the temperature of a cup of warm water every 2 minutes for 10 minutes (or record the temperature outside each hour). Plot the points on a line graph and join them. Talk about the trend.
days.en: Plan a formal letter to the head teacher or a local council asking for something special (a new bench, a school garden). List three reasons, each for its own paragraph.

days.ma: Chart questions: from your bar chart, ask 'How many more chose apples than pears?' 'How many people altogether?' Then interpret a chart from a newspaper or fact book.
days.en: Draft the letter in standard English, with a paragraph for each reason, fronted adverbials ('Firstly,' 'In addition,') and polite language. Check 'we were' and 'I did'.

days.ma: Tables and pictograms: make a pictogram of the number of books on each shelf (1 picture = 2 books). Then a table of pocket money saved over 4 weeks; find the total and difference.
days.en: Spelling: add dis-, mis-, un- or re- to appointment, understand, believable and consider. Learn special and popular and use both in the letter.

days.ma: Friday check: read your bar chart and answer three questions; from a time graph, say what the temperature was at 4 minutes; make a table from given data. Mark together and discuss.
days.en: Dictation: 'Firstly, we would like a special bench.' and 'Is the school garden popular?' Then finish and sign the letter.

weeks.title: Consolidation: decimals, money, time and data

spell.rule: Revise this half term: -ly, homophones, y and ou, word families and prefixes

weeks.read: A book your child chooses for the half-term break; keep a reading log of minutes read each day.

days.ma: Decimals and money: order £1.05, £1.50, £0.15, £10.50; round 6.7 kg and 3.2 m to the nearest whole; 'A pen costs £1.35. How much for 4?' Show working.
days.en: Spelling round-up: read 10 words (gently, basically, potatoes, mystery, knowledge, strength, special, popular, probably, naughty). Your child writes them; tick and practise any slips.

days.ma: Time mix: convert 14:25 to 12-hour time; 3 weeks to days; 150 minutes to hours and minutes. 'A train leaves at 09:45 and arrives at 11:20. How long is the journey?'
days.en: Edit the letter from last week: check paragraphs, standard English and commas after fronted adverbials. Write out a neat final copy with separate paragraphs.

days.ma: Data: make a bar chart of how long each family member spends reading in a day. Ask and answer three comparison questions. Then times tables practice: 25 questions, 6 seconds each, like the national check in June.
days.en: Write a short poem or set of instructions about how to look after a pet. Use a heading, numbered steps or stanzas and at least two fronted adverbials.

days.ma: Problem day: 'Tickets cost £4.50 for adults and £2.25 for children. How much for 2 adults and 3 children? What change from £20?'
days.en: Proof-read the poem or instructions, checking spellings with a dictionary. Then copy one section in best handwriting with parallel downstrokes.

days.ma: Half-term check: 12 mixed questions on comparing and rounding decimals, money, time and charts. Then a timed tables round. Celebrate and note anything to revisit.
days.en: Dictation: '"Keep the cats in separate rooms," warned the vet.' and 'At 18:00, we were reading.' Check the inverted commas, the comma after the fronted adverbial and the spelling of separate.

weeks.title: Angles, triangles and quadrilaterals

spell.rule: Suffixes -ment, -ness, -ful and -less, including changing y to i (enjoyment, happiness, plentiful, merciless, loneliness)

weeks.read: A non-chronological report (an information book about an animal group, a country or a planet) to use as a model.

days.ma: Make a right-angle checker by folding a scrap of paper twice. Hunt for angles around the home: are they right angles, acute (smaller) or obtuse (bigger, but less than two right angles)? Record five of each.
days.en: Start a non-chronological report unit. Read a report about an animal group together. Notice that it is organised by topic (habitat, diet, appearance) not by time, with headings, present tense and technical words.

days.ma: Order angles: draw five angles on paper (or open a book or scissors to different angles). Order them from smallest to largest and label acute, right and obtuse. Talk about what a straight line (two right angles) is.
days.en: Retrieve and sort: make notes from the report under three headings. Then explain the purpose of the report and how the layout helps the reader find information.

days.ma: Triangles: draw or cut out equilateral, isosceles, scalene and right-angled triangles. Sort them by sides and by angles. Can a triangle have two right angles? Why not?
days.en: Spelling: add -ment, -ness, -ful or -less to enjoy, happy, plenty, mercy and lonely, changing y to i where needed. Learn purpose.

days.ma: Quadrilaterals: draw a square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, trapezium and kite. Sort them by parallel sides, equal sides and right angles in a table. Then times tables check practice: 25 questions, 6 seconds each.
days.en: Plan your own report on an animal group or a topic you know well. Choose four headings, write the facts you know, and find two more facts from a book. Use terms such as 'heading', 'paragraph' and 'technical vocabulary'.

days.ma: Friday check: name an acute, an obtuse and a right angle in the room; order three drawn angles; which quadrilateral has exactly one pair of parallel sides? Sort four triangles. Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'The purpose of the report is to share facts.' and 'Hedgehogs are plentiful in hedges and gardens.' Check full stops and the suffix spellings.

weeks.title: Lines of symmetry

spell.rule: Apostrophes: plural (dogs), singular possessive (dog's), plural possessive (dogs') and contraction (it's), plus its with no apostrophe

weeks.read: Carry on with the information books; choose one with diagrams or photos showing symmetry in nature.

days.ma: Fold paper shapes (square, rectangle, equilateral triangle, a heart, a letter H) to find lines of symmetry. Record how many each has. Does a rectangle have diagonal lines of symmetry? Test it by folding.
days.en: Draft the introduction and first section of the report. Use the present tense, a general opening ('Owls are birds of prey that …'), sub-headings and technical words with a short explanation.

days.ma: Symmetry in different orientations: draw shapes turned on their side or upside down (a kite, an arrow, a diamond). Use a small mirror or fold to find the lines of symmetry. Turning a shape does not change its symmetry.
days.en: Draft two more sections. Use paragraphs with one main idea each, and conjunctions such as 'although' and 'because' to explain. Check pronouns refer clearly to the right noun.

days.ma: Complete a symmetric figure: on squared paper, draw a vertical line and half a pattern or shape on one side. Your child completes the mirror image. Then try a horizontal line.
days.en: Apostrophe sort: write the dogs, the dog's, the dogs', it's and its in sentences with gaps. Your child chooses the right one. Learn suppose and write 'I suppose the dogs' bowls are empty.'

days.ma: Symmetry walk: look for symmetrical things at home or outside (windows, leaves, butterflies in photos, letters on signs). Sketch three and draw their lines of symmetry. Then 25 tables questions, 6 seconds each.
days.en: Homophones review: write a short paragraph for your report that uses their, there and they're correctly, and check any other homophones you have used.

days.ma: Friday check: how many lines of symmetry does a square have? A rectangle? An equilateral triangle? Complete a symmetric shape on squared paper. Which letters of the alphabet have a line of symmetry? Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'I suppose it's the owls' nest.' and 'The owl stretched its wings.' Talk through each apostrophe choice.

weeks.title: Coordinates and plotting shapes

spell.rule: Homophone review: whose/who's, there/their/they're, here/hear, peace/piece, weather/whether

weeks.read: A book with maps (an atlas, a story map at the front of an adventure book, or a local map).

days.ma: Draw a grid on squared paper numbered 0 to 10 along the bottom (x-axis) and up the side (y-axis). Plot points such as (3, 5) and (7, 2), remembering 'along the corridor, then up the stairs'.
days.en: Edit the report: read it aloud. Is each section under the right heading? Add a fact box or diagram with labels, and check every sentence is in the present tense.

days.ma: Treasure map: draw a simple island on a 0 to 10 grid and hide treasure at a secret coordinate. Your partner guesses coordinates; you say 'warmer' or 'colder'. Swap.
days.en: Proof-read the report line by line. Check homophones, apostrophes and commas after fronted adverbials. Use a dictionary for any uncertain spellings.

days.ma: Plot and complete: plot (2, 2), (2, 6) and (6, 6). What fourth point makes a square? Then plot three corners of a rectangle and find the fourth. Join the points with a ruler.
days.en: Spelling: fill gaps in sentences with whose/who's, there/their/they're, here/hear, peace/piece and weather/whether. Learn therefore and perhaps.

days.ma: Shape coordinates: draw a triangle, a kite and a parallelogram on the grid and write the coordinates of every vertex. Read them to your partner, who plots them to see if they make the same shapes.
days.en: Present the report: read it aloud to the family as if you were an expert on a nature programme, speaking clearly and adding expression to the most surprising facts.

days.ma: Friday check: write the coordinates of 4 points on a grid; plot (0, 4) and (4, 0); find the missing vertex of a square at (1, 1), (1, 4), (4, 4). Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: 'Perhaps there is treasure, therefore we must dig.' and 'Whose map shows their island?' Check the commas and homophones.

weeks.title: Translations on a grid

spell.rule: Choosing the right ending: -tion, -sion, -ssion or -cian; and -ous review (decision, position, expression, optician, famous, curious)

weeks.read: A story with a surprising ending; talk about how the writer kept it hidden until the end.

days.ma: Translation means sliding a shape without turning it. Draw a small triangle on a grid and translate it 3 squares right and 2 squares up. Record the new coordinates of each corner.
days.en: Read a story with a surprise ending. Before the end, predict how it will finish using clues. After reading, discuss which clues were hidden in the text.

days.ma: Describe moves: place a button on a grid. Your partner gives instructions such as '4 left, 1 down'. Then work backwards: give a start and end coordinate, and describe the translation.
days.en: Discuss the story: why did the characters act as they did? Find evidence for one character's motive. Take turns to share opinions and build on what the other person says.

days.ma: Board game design: on a 10 by 10 grid, draw a path. Write movement cards ('2 right, 3 up'). Play with buttons as counters and record the coordinates of each move.
days.en: Spelling: decide the ending for decide, position, express, optic, fame and curious. Learn material and use it in a sentence about clothes.

days.ma: Translate a shape: plot a rectangle at (1, 1), (1, 3), (4, 3), (4, 1). Translate it 5 right and 4 up. What happens to every x and y coordinate? Then times tables practice: 25 questions.
days.en: Write a new surprise ending for the story, including dialogue. Check direct speech punctuation and use a fronted adverbial for drama ('Without warning,').

days.ma: Friday check: a point at (3, 2) moves 4 right and 3 up – where does it end? Describe the translation from (6, 5) to (2, 7). Translate a small triangle on a grid. Mark together.
days.en: Dictation: '"What material is this?" asked the curious optician.' and 'Without warning, the famous magician vanished.' Check inverted commas and the endings.

weeks.title: Review: number, calculation and times tables

spell.rule: Review autumn and spring rules: in-/im-/il-/ir-, sc, -ous, -tion/-sion/-ssion/-cian, plural possessive apostrophes, inter-/sub-/super-/anti-/auto-

weeks.read: A joke or riddle book – fun reading that plays with word meanings and homophones.

days.ma: Place value game: draw four digit cards and make the largest and smallest numbers. Round each to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000, and find the difference between them in columns.
days.en: Spelling review: your child writes 20 words learned this year from the autumn and spring lists. Make a list of any to practise with look–say–cover–write–check.

days.ma: Calculation challenge: 4768 + 3457 and 8006 – 3769, each with an estimate and inverse check. Then make up a two-step problem for a grown-up.
days.en: Grammar check-up: write one sentence each with a fronted adverbial, direct speech, a plural possessive apostrophe, an expanded noun phrase and standard English 'we were'.

days.ma: Times tables mixed 12 × 12 grid: fill in as many as you can in 5 minutes. Then 25 × 4 × 3; factor pairs of 36; 63 ÷ 7; 0 × 99.
days.en: Read jokes and riddles aloud. Find ones using homophones or words with two meanings, and explain why they are funny.

days.ma: Problem solving: 'A theatre has 14 rows of 9 seats and sells 87 tickets. How many seats are empty?' Then '6 times as many children as adults; there are 8 adults. How many people?'
days.en: Write five jokes or riddles of your own. Proof-read them, check tricky spellings in a dictionary and copy the best in neat handwriting.

days.ma: Review check: 12 mixed number questions from the year (place value, rounding, negatives, Roman numerals, column methods, tables, 3-digit × 1-digit). Celebrate progress.
days.en: Dictation: 'I believe the various riddles were certain to make us laugh.' and '"Don't mention the joke!" said the women.' Check apostrophes and inverted commas.

weeks.title: Review: fractions, decimals, measures, shape and data

spell.rule: Review summer rules: -ly, homophones, y and ou, word families, prefixes dis-/mis-/un-/re-, suffixes -ment/-ness/-ful/-less

weeks.read: A mixture of fiction and non-fiction chosen by your child at the library.

days.ma: Fractions and decimals: equivalent fractions to 2/3; 5/8 + 2/8; 3/5 of 40; 3/4 as a decimal; order 0.3, 0.33, 0.03. Draw a diagram for one of them.
days.en: Spelling review: 20 words from the summer lists. Use a dictionary to check any that are uncertain.

days.ma: Measures and money: find the perimeter and area of a rectangle on squared paper; convert 2 km to m and 3 hours to minutes; 'A drink is £1.35 – change from £5?'
days.en: Read a story chapter and answer three questions: one fact, one about a character's feelings with evidence, one prediction.

days.ma: Time: convert 16:40 to 12-hour time; 'A film starts at 18:45 and lasts 1 hour 50 minutes. When does it end?'; how many days in 9 weeks?
days.en: Retrieval: from a non-fiction book, make a five-question quiz for the family, with an answer key.

days.ma: Shape and position: classify three triangles and three quadrilaterals; find acute and obtuse angles in the room; plot a shape on a grid and translate it 3 right and 2 down. Then make a bar chart of family shoe sizes and ask two questions.
days.en: Proof-read a piece of writing from earlier in the year. Correct spellings, add missing apostrophes and improve two word choices. Explain each change.

days.ma: Review check: 12 mixed questions on fractions, decimals, measures, money, time, shape, coordinates and charts. Celebrate progress and note any to revisit.
days.en: Dictation: 'Occasionally, the children's knowledge was put under pressure.' and 'It's the girls' prized possession.' Check apostrophes and the comma.

weeks.title: Fun project: design a back-garden treasure trail

spell.rule: Spelling celebration: choose 10 favourite words from this year's list and make a crossword with clues

weeks.read: Your child's choice – a favourite book from the year to re-read and recommend.

days.ma: Map it: draw a map of the garden, a room or a local park on a 0 to 10 grid. Choose 5 clue spots and write their coordinates. Describe the moves from one to the next as translations.
days.en: Plan the treasure trail: who it is for, where it will be and what the treasure is. Look at puzzle books or game instructions for ideas and note how clues are worded.

days.ma: Measure it: measure the distances between clue spots in metres and centimetres, and the perimeter of the trail area. Convert the total to centimetres and estimate how many steps it is.
days.en: Write five clues, each a riddle or a coded message, using expanded noun phrases and fronted adverbials ('Under the special stone, …'). Include at least one homophone joke.

days.ma: Time it and budget it: plan a timetable using 24-hour times for setting up, playing and a snack break. Plan a pretend £10 budget for prizes using prices from a leaflet. Show the change.
days.en: Write instructions for players: a title, 'You will need', numbered steps with commands, and a rules box. Edit for clarity and proof-read spellings.

days.ma: Data: after a practice run, record how long each player takes in a table and draw a bar chart. Who was fastest? What is the difference between the fastest and slowest?
days.en: Book recommendation: write a short review of your favourite book of the year (what it is about, the best part, who would enjoy it). Share it and discuss.

days.ma: Play the trail with the family, keeping to the timetable. Finish with a 10-question quiz covering the whole year, with a tables round of 12 questions. Celebrate the year!
days.en: Celebration: read aloud your favourite piece of writing from the year to the family with expression. Talk about how your writing has changed and set one goal for Year 5.
